content: Lead(II) nitrate is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Pb(NO3)2. It typically appears as colorless crystals or a white powder. Unlike most other lead(II) salts, it is soluble in water. Historically, it was known as plumb dulcis during the Middle Ages. Its production involved reacting metallic lead or lead oxide with nitric acid, but this was done on a small scale for the preparation of other lead compounds. By the 19th century, lead(II) nitrate began to be produced commercially in Europe and the United States. Its primary historical use was as a raw material for pigments in lead-based paints, such as chrome yellow and chrome orange. However, these paints have largely been replaced by less toxic alternatives, such as those based on titanium dioxide. Other industrial applications included its use as a heat stabilizer in nylon and polyesters, as well as in coatings for photothermographic paper. Since around 2000, lead(II) nitrate has also been used in the gold cyanidation process. Lead(II) nitrate is toxic, acts as an oxidizing agent, and is classified as probably carcinogenic to humans by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). As a result, strict safety precautions are necessary to prevent inhalation, ingestion, or skin contact. Its hazardous nature has led to ongoing scrutiny of its limited applications. The compound has been known since the Middle Ages, primarily for its role in producing pigments for lead-based paints. These pigments were used in dyeing and printing textiles. The German alchemist Andreas Libavius first described lead(II) nitrate in 1597, naming it plumb dulcis or sweet lead due to its taste. Over the centuries, its property of decrepitation (crackling upon heating) led to its use in matches and specialized explosives like lead azide. The production process involves dissolving lead in nitric acid, yielding lead(II) nitrate crystals. Despite its straightforward synthesis, large-scale production was not reported until 1835. By 1974, the U.S. consumption of lead compounds, excluding pigments and gasoline additives, was 642 tonnes. Lead(II) nitrate dissolves readily in water, dissociating into lead(II) cations and nitrate anions. When mixed with a solution containing iodide ions, it forms a bright orange-yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide. This reaction is often used in educational demonstrations due to the striking color change. Similar reactions occur in the solid phase when finely ground mixtures of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide are combined. The resulting color depends on the proportions of the reactants and the extent of grinding. Lead(II) nitrate is one of the few soluble lead compounds, alongside lead(II) acetate. Most other lead compounds, such as lead halides (chloride, bromide, iodide), are only weakly soluble in water. This makes lead(II) nitrate a key starting material for producing insoluble lead compounds through double decomposition reactions. For example, hot solutions of lead halides can be cooled to form iridescent crystals, with colors depending on the halide (white for chloride, buff for bromide, yellow for iodide). These phenomena are often used in classroom demonstrations of solubility. When concentrated sodium hydroxide is added to a lead(II) nitrate solution, basic lead nitrates are formed. Up to the half-equivalence point, Pb(NO3)2·Pb(OH)2 predominates, while beyond this point, Pb(NO3)2·5Pb(OH)2 is formed. Simple lead(II) hydroxide (Pb(OH)2) does not form, even at pH levels as high as 12. The crystal structure of lead(II) nitrate has been determined using neutron diffraction. It crystallizes in a cubic system, with lead atoms arranged in a face-centered cubic lattice. Each lead atom is coordinated to twelve oxygen atoms, with a bond length of 281 picometers. The nitrate groups are positioned above and below the plane of the lead atoms. All N–O bond lengths are identical at 127 picometers. Research into the crystal structure has explored the possibility of free internal rotation of the nitrate groups at elevated temperatures, but this has not been observed. Lead(II) nitrate exhibits interesting supramolecular chemistry due to its ability to coordinate with nitrogen and oxygen electron-donating compounds. For example, combining lead nitrate with pentaethylene glycol in a solution of acetonitrile and methanol produces a crystalline material where the glycol chain wraps around the lead ion in a crown ether-like configuration. The lead ion adopts a bicapped square antiprism geometry with a coordination number of 10. Other complexes, such as those formed with bithiazole ligands, exhibit asymmetry in the coordination sphere, likely due to the presence of a lone pair of electrons on the lead ion. As an oxidizing agent, lead(II) nitrate can participate in redox reactions. Its Pb2+ ion has a standard reduction potential of −0.125 V, while the nitrate ion has a potential of +0.956 V under acidic conditions. When heated, lead(II) nitrate decomposes into lead(II) oxide, oxygen gas, and nitrogen dioxide, producing a crackling sound (decrepitation). This property makes it useful in pyrotechnics, such as fireworks. Lead(II) nitrate is not found naturally and is typically synthesized by dissolving metallic lead or lead(II) oxide in nitric acid. The resulting solution yields anhydrous crystals of lead(II) nitrate. Commercially, it is supplied in various quantities, from laboratory containers to large industrial bags. Impure solutions of lead(II) nitrate are also generated as by-products in the processing of lead-containing wastes, such as lead–bismuth residues from refineries. These solutions are sometimes used in gold cyanidation. Due to its toxicity, lead(II) nitrate has been largely replaced in many applications. For example, titanium dioxide has supplanted lead-based pigments in paints. Its use in matches and fireworks has also declined. Current applications include its role as a heat stabilizer in nylon and polyesters, as a coating for photothermographic paper, and in rodenticides. In laboratories, lead(II) nitrate is a convenient source of dinitrogen tetroxide (N2O4). By carefully drying and heating lead(II) nitrate, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and oxygen are produced. Alternatively, NO2 can be generated by reacting concentrated nitric acid with copper turnings. The resulting gas mixture can be condensed and fractionally distilled to separate NO2 and N2O4, with the latter favored at low temperatures. In gold cyanidation, lead(II) nitrate is added to improve the leaching process. Only small amounts (10–100 milligrams per kilogram of gold) are required. However, both the cyanidation process and the use of lead compounds are controversial due to their environmental and health risks. Lead(II) nitrate is highly toxic, and ingestion can result in acute lead poisoning. All soluble lead compounds are classified as probably carcinogenic to humans (Category 2A) by the IARC. They have been linked to renal cancer, glioma, and other cancers in both humans and experimental animals. Lead interferes with enzymes such as δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase and pyrimidine-5′-nucleotidase, disrupting heme biosynthesis and DNA metabolism. Spills and environmental release must be avoided, and all waste must be disposed of as hazardous material.
